7.0.s.en: (1) The advance of Holofernes upon Bethulia

7.0.0.en: The next day: after the day on which Achior was bound to the tree and delivered to Bethulia. Holofernes gave his orders to his armies to move toward Judea to fight the children of Israel, so they advanced toward Bethulia. This was on the morning of the day that the people had spent in prayer and fasting until night, so the people rested only a few hours before they saw the Assyrian advance coming against them. Perhaps this was the opposite of what the Jews expected, since they thought that God's answer would be to keep the Assyrian army away from them, but it was the wisdom of God, which will appear later.

7.1.1.en: Those taken from the captured lands: the men whom Holofernes took captive from the lands he occupied and added to his army to fight with him.

7.1.3.en: Holofernes gave his orders to his armies to move toward Judea to fight the children of Israel, and the great army moved, of which the Holy Bible states that the number of foot soldiers in it was one hundred and twenty thousand and the number of horsemen twenty-two thousand, in addition to several thousand soldiers who joined the army of the Assyrians from the lands Holofernes had occupied, so that the number of his army increased greatly and was hard to count, while it was not to be expected that the soldiers of the small city of Bethulia would exceed a thousand soldiers. This shows the impossibility of Bethulia triumphing over the Assyrians except by the power of God, which works miracles. It is to be noted that the number of horsemen mentioned in the text is twenty-two thousand, although the number mentioned in (ch. 2:7) is twelve thousand, but the translation of the Jesuit Fathers states in the seventh chapter that the number of horsemen is twelve thousand, so perhaps the figure of twenty-two thousand is an error in the translation we have, or in copying.

7.2.0.en: This mighty army moved forward to Judea from the north by way of the plain of Esdraelon, which is a triangular plain lying between Galilee and Samaria, twelve miles long from north to south and twenty-five miles wide from the river Jordan to the Mediterranean Sea. Then it advanced toward a place called Cyamon, heading for the city of Bethulia, which lies on a mountain and was the first of the cities that Holofernes met when he entered Judea. His army encamped in a valley lying between Cyamon in the north and Bethulia in the south (that is, lengthwise), and in breadth it lies between Belmaim and the hill of Dothan, which overlooks its plain. In this valley the sight of the army – whose number reached tens of thousands – was fearful and mighty.

7.2.1.en: Holofernes moved with his mighty army, confident in himself that he would shatter those small lands, the first of which was Bethulia, and he did not know that there could be a power greater than he, namely the power of God, which supports the weak. Do not rely on yourself and forget God when facing problems and in your relations with others, but rely on God and have confidence in your soul that relies on Him, and you will be at peace all the days of your life.

7.3.0.en: When the people of God in Bethulia looked from their city on the mountain at the valley before them and saw this great army, they were very afraid, so they hurried to God, prostrating themselves in reverence, and even put ashes on their heads in humility before Him, and prayed with supplication to God to have mercy on them and rescue them from the Assyrians.

7.4.1.en: The soldiers of Bethulia hurried to guard the places leading to the pass between the two mountains that led to the city, for it was the only entrance to the city on the mountain, and they organized an armed guard through the night and day. Thus prayers went up and were mingled with the watch; that is, they took refuge in God and did their duty at the same time.

7.4.2.en: Do not be dismayed before the multitude of the wicked, but take refuge in your God by prayer and supplication in humility and lowliness, confident in His mercies, and at the same time do your duty with all faithfulness, so that you are one who trusts in God and not one who is merely idle in reliance on Him. Guard the entrances of your heart, that is, your senses, so that evil does not enter through them, and let your spiritual wakefulness be constant night and day, and when God sees your striving He will keep you from every sin.

7.5.s.en: (2) Holofernes cuts off the water from the city

7.5.0.en: When Holofernes saw that the city was fortified, he began to go around it to learn how to attack it. He was passing on his horse with a group of horsemen, and they found outside the city on the south the main spring of water, which supplied the city, and from which a channel came out and entered into the city. So he knew that it was the main source of the water that fed the city, and he commanded that the channel be blocked, and by this he cut off the water entering the city, that the people of Bethulia might die of thirst. The water channel emptied inside the city into a deep pit, which was considered as a reservoir of water, from which it was afterward drawn up into basins for people and animals to drink.

7.6.0.en: After cutting off the water coming from the main spring that fed the city, there remained only a very few springs of water inside the city, and a few springs outside the city beside its walls. When the main source of water was cut off, the water inside the city was no longer sufficient for the needs of the people, so some of the people would go out secretly from the gates of the city and fill from these nearby springs, despite the danger of exposing themselves to the violence of the soldiers of Holofernes. Of course this water was not enough to quench the thirst of all the people, and they began to suffer from lack of water.

7.7.0.en: Fence them in: surround them and protect them.

7.7.1.en: Distress: extreme affliction that is close to death.

7.7.2.en: Valleys: plural of the ravine, that is, the valley.

7.7.4.en: Then the Moabites and the children of Ammon came forward, the peoples neighboring the children of Israel despite the physical kinship between them, for they are descendants of Lot, the nephew of Abraham, the father of the Jewish people, but they were hostile to them because they were pagans, whereas the Jews worshiped God. Here the cunning and craftiness of Holofernes appear in enlisting the Moabites and the Ammonites to help him in fighting the children of Israel, because they were their enemies. This was a custom known anciently in war, such as Pilate's use of the Samaritans to suppress the revolts of the Jews in Jerusalem and Judea.

7.7.5.en: When they saw Holofernes preparing to attack the city, they gloated over the Jews, and even hurried to give advice to Holofernes so that the people of Bethulia might perish. They said to him that the Jews who dwell in Bethulia rely on their city being fortified on the top of the mountain, and the mountains surround and protect it, so they do not rely for the defense of their city on the known weapons such as the sword and the spear, and you can destroy them without war by watching the springs near the walls so that they cannot draw water from them secretly.

7.7.6.en: The devil in his war with the children of God hems them in at the main sources of their livelihood, so that they fall into poverty, sickness and many troubles, hoping that they will leave God.

7.7.7.en: The wicked may also gather together when they find the children of God in calamity, to make their affliction harder by narrowing their sources of livelihood, even the secondary ones, to make sure of their destruction, and they advise their enemies to destroy them, hoping by this to win honor, or some gifts, from these enemies.

7.7.8.en: Do not fear the one who has authority to harm your body, for first, he cannot harm you unless God permits him, and only to the extent that He permits; and he also cannot touch your spirit. God permits this to see the extent of your steadfastness in the faith and your endurance of afflictions, and be confident that in the end He will give you victory over your enemies and will not permit your destruction.

7.7.9.en: Do not be dismayed when the wicked gather against you, even if they are your relatives, for they are nothing before the power of God who protects you, and even if they take from you the sources of your livelihood, God will provide for you in miraculous ways.

7.8.0.en: Holofernes was pleased with their idea and set soldiers to guard these springs and kill anyone who approached them. He was strict, so he set over each spring a company of a hundred soldiers to prevent any attempt by Bethulia to draw water secretly.

7.9.0.en: Their cisterns: that is, their basins, the plural of basin.

7.9.1.en: Holofernes continued his guarding of all the springs of water outside the walls of the city of Bethulia, so that only a few wells of water remained and some collections of water, that is, the basins connected to these wells. The quantity of water in them was not enough for the people, although it was distributed to each family in small measure, and after twenty days it almost dried up, and what remained of it was barely enough for one day.

7.10.s.en: (3) The thirst of the people and their demand to surrender the city

7.10.0.en: When the thirst of the people increased and they began to faint and were about to depart from life, a power to preserve their survival stirred in them, so they rose in anger in all their groups – men, women, elders and children – and seized Ozias the head of the city and began to blame him violently, because he refused to come to terms with the Assyrians and surrender the city to them. Their sense of their life slipping away from them made them forget their faith in God and their love for Ozias the head of their city, so they rebuked him severely, ascribing the fault to him, although they had been convinced of the preparation for war, the fervent prayer and the tears they had poured out before God. But all this collapsed before the confrontation with death.

7.11.2.en: The people expressed their condition by saying that they were dying slowly of thirst, and having lost their faith in God, they said that they had no one to rescue them and support them in their trial.

7.11.3.en: When affliction grows severe upon you, instead of falling into despair and anger at others and directing accusations at them, I wish that you would hasten and cast your troubles at the feet of Christ, for He feels for you, and is nearer to you than at any other time, and is ready to help you.

7.12.0.en: Facing the fear of death, the foremost of the people asked Ozias to call everyone in the city to go out to Holofernes and surrender themselves to him, so that they would become slaves and captives, in order to escape death.

7.13.0.en: The people felt that surrendering themselves to Holofernes would give them life, and that this was better, because life is better than death, since they could worship God and bless Him with many prayers while alive, but if they remained in the city they would die and lose their ability to pray, and would be tormented by seeing their children and women die before their eyes, and in the end they themselves would die also. How cruel death is, for facing death is hard. When a person feels death creeping up to master him, he is greatly disturbed, especially if he sees with his own eyes the death of his children, for they are dearer to him than himself, so he defends them out of the instinct of motherhood or fatherhood, to the point that some people rush to kill their children so as not to see them die before their eyes.

7.14.0.en: Our end: the end of our life.

7.14.1.en: The burning of thirst: very severe thirst.

7.14.2.en: Then they pressed Ozias and the elders of the city and tried to extract from them a promise and an oath to surrender the city and those in it to Holofernes, and they declared that they were sinners and that the affliction that came upon them was divine discipline. They even said that quick death by the sword at the hand of Holofernes was better than dying of thirst, because quick death by the sword does not torment a person like slow death by thirst; that is, they were determined in every case to surrender themselves to the Assyrians, whether they spared their lives or killed them. This shows the extent of their despair and the weakness of their faith.

7.14.3.en: I wish that affliction would lead us to hold fast to God, and that according to our attachment to the spiritual life we would endure material afflictions and remain steadfast in our faith, not accepting slavery to sin or delivering our life to Satan, for to die while we are pure and free from sin is better than to live while we are drowned in evils.

7.15.0.en: Wailing: weeping with a loud voice.

7.15.1.en: Fainted: fell to the ground in extreme exhaustion.

7.15.3.en: From the despair of the people and the difficulty of their facing death by thirst, they showed their distress with Ozias and accused him of being the cause of their destruction and demanded that he surrender the city. But their faith was still alive, though weak, so they took refuge in God, their only refuge, with prayer, crying and tears for long hours, and they even offered common prayers with one voice, showing the oneness of their feelings. The following appeared in their prayers:

7.15.4.en: 1- Their repentance and their confession of their faults and the faults of their fathers. Repentance is the first thing by which we draw out the mercies of God. Their remembrance of the sins of their fathers goes back to a mistaken belief that was prevalent among the Jews, that children are punished because of the sins of their fathers, but God made clear the error of this belief in (Ex 18:2-4).

7.15.5.en: 2- Their hoping for the mercies of God to rescue them from their enemies.

7.15.6.en: 3- Since their faults deserve punishment, if God sees fit to punish them, let Him punish them Himself and not deliver them into the hands of their enemies. Here they imitate David the prophet who said, "Let us fall now into the hand of the Lord; for his mercies are great: and let me not fall into the hand of man" (2 Sam 24:14).

7.15.7.en: 4- Their asking that God would rescue them and be glorified in them, so that the power of God would appear before all the peoples, instead of its being said that God had left them if Holofernes stormed them. From the abundance of their crying and prayers they grew weary and in the end fell silent, with their hearts speaking instead of their lips, and they waited for the mercies of God and His help. Thus by repentance, faith and prayers to God, putting their hope in Him and not in the pagan gods, they were able to draw out the mercies of God, and they offered complete striving unto death.

7.15.8.en: I wish that we would take refuge in God before everything, because none other than He loves us and is able to save us. And as long as we come before Him with repentance and humility, we shall surely obtain His mercies, even if He permits our punishment, for He is merciful and does not leave us to perish, and in the end the name of God is glorified in us.

7.16.0.en: Finally Ozias spoke, the head of the city and the one responsible for leading this people.

7.16.1.en: Here wise leadership appears: he was not disturbed by their accusation of him, nor angry with them, but shared their feelings, their prayers, their crying and their tears, and felt his responsibility, so he stood with them to reassure them of the presence of God. Then he took a spiritual decision better than what they had asked, for he asked them to wait five days, in prayers, to see God's intervention and His deliverance of them, instead of surrendering the city at once as they asked. And if God did not intervene, then after five days he would surrender the city.

7.16.2.en: Perhaps he asked their permission to wait five days because he knew that the small quantity of water in the city could suffice for them for five days, and by this the extent of Ozias' holding to endurance appears, to the utmost that the people could bear. It is striving unto death, that is, to the utmost possible striving, as the New Testament teaches us to strive unto blood (Heb 12:4)

7.16.3.en: How beautiful it is that you bear your responsibility, whether as the head of a family, or as a servant in the Church, or as one responsible in any work, so that you care for those with you and bear with their faults and encourage them and guide them spiritually. Care also for your own spiritual life, so that your spiritual stature and your faith may grow, and you may be able to carry out the tasks of your service and your responsibility. According to the spiritual stature of the servant he is able to guide and lead his people spiritually.

7.16.4.en: It is evident that Ozias had a spiritual stature greater than his people. Though a greater spiritual stature will appear afterward in Judith, not only than the people, but than all the elders of the city and than Ozias himself.

7.16.5.en: The faith of Judith and her rebuke of the elders (1) The character of Judith (vv. 1-8:)

7.16.6.en: 1- And when Judith the widow heard these words, who was the daughter of Merari the son of Idus, the son of Joseph, the son of Ozias, the son of Elai, the son of Minor, the son of Gideon, the son of Raphaim, the son of Ahitub, the son of Malchiah, the son of Hanan, the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Mashon, the son of Reuben. 2- And her husband was Manasseh, and he died in the days of the barley harvest. 3- For as he stood over those that bound the sheaves in the field, the heat struck his head, and he died in Bethulia his city, and was buried there with his fathers. 4- And Judith had remained a widow three years and six months. 5- And she had prepared for herself a secret chamber at the top of her house, and she dwelt in it with her maidservants and kept it shut. 6- And she had sackcloth upon her loins, and she fasted all the days of her life, except the sabbaths and the new moons and the feasts of the house of Israel. 7- And she was of a very beautiful countenance, and her husband had left her great riches and many servants and possessions full of herds of oxen and flocks of sheep. 8- And she had a good report among all people, because she feared the Lord greatly, and there was none that spoke an ill word of her.
